transcript:
HEADER:
Date: 2026-12-01
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Carlos Rivera (HarborTrust Head of ML), Priya Singh (HarborTrust Platform), Evelyn Park (HarborTrust SRE)
Artifacts referenced: benchmark spreadsheet (https://redwood.app/benchmarks/harbortrust-2026-11-30), streaming test plan (link in notes), SOC2/VPC checklist (redwood.com/security)

Summary: quick sync on POC latency tuning. Reviewed TTFT (time-to-first-token) numbers, streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, sequence length profile from HarborTrust, and kernel choices. Agreed to run a focused streaming test with short-prefix caching and to try kernel tweak for seq len 512. Next steps and owners captured.

TOPICS: TTFT targets, streaming, prefix/KV cache warming, sequence length distribution, kernel selection/quantization, dedicated vs hosted latency tradeoffs, SOC2/VPC checklist request.

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on a Tuesday, we really appreciate the time. Quick check, audio ok?
[00:05] Carlos Rivera: Yep, all good. Thanks Maya.
[00:08] Liam O'Connor: Hey folks, Liam here, I'll be driving the perf notes today.
[00:12] Priya Singh: Hi, yep, Priya on platform. We pushed the traces overnight, you should have them in the sheet.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Great, I saw the upload, thanks. So agenda - go over benchmark numbers, dig into TTFT and p95, talk streaming, kernel choices, and agree next steps.
[00:28] Carlos Rivera: Sounds good. Our main goal is sub-200ms TTFT for short prompts and p95 under 350ms, that's our internal SLO for the customer-facing flows.
[00:37] Liam O'Connor: Great, that's helpful. Quick context from our side: last run (sheet v3) shows p50 TTFT ~180ms for hosted small-batched runs, p95 closer to 420ms when we hit cold KV cache and padding overhead.
[00:49] Evelyn Park: When you say cold KV cache, you're talking about the per-session key-value cache on the GPU warm-up, right?
[00:54] Liam O'Connor: Yeah that's right. There are two modes we consider: cold path where KV cache isn't warmed by prior requests, and warmed/prefix-cached where we store prefix keys and rehydrate (we call it prefix caching). Warmed path drops p95 substantially.
[01:10] Priya Singh: Our workload has a heavy tail - most requests are 16-64 tokens, but around 10-12% are long-form 512+ due to multi-turn context. Sequence length distribution attached in the sheet.
[01:22] Maya Chen: That distribution explains some of the p95 variance — a few long seqs will balloon batching and kernel scheduling.
[01:28] Carlos Rivera: Okay, so what's the recommended approach? We are considering running Dedicated but still want to confirm if hosted with tuning is feasible.
[01:36] Liam O'Connor: Two levers: 1) enable streaming to start returning tokens faster (lowers TTFT significantly for UX), 2) tune kernel/compilation choices to optimize for your most common seq lengths. Streaming + prefix caching usually gets TTFT down under 150ms for short prompts on our verified models.
[01:50] Priya Singh: Is there a cost tradeoff with streaming? I thought streaming prevented some batching gains.
[01:54] Liam O'Connor: Right, there's a trade: streaming reduces effective batching because we flush earlier to send partial tokens, so throughput can drop unless you use micro-batching and async I/O. But for your SLO (latency-sensitive UI) streaming is usually worth it. We also use partial token aggregation to keep some throughput.
[02:08] Carlos Rivera: For kernel choices, you mentioned earlier you run an internal selection between cutlass-like kernels vs our other path, can you clarify?
[02:15] Liam O'Connor: Yeah, shorthand: our runtime picks different matrix-mul kernels and attention implementations depending on sequence length and hardware. For sequence len <=128 we pick small-matmul kernels (lower overhead), for 256-512 we switch to medium kernels with different tiling, and beyond that we pick the large-kernel path. We can override selection to favor the 512 path if most requests are in that bucket, reduces overhead of switching.
[02:36] Evelyn Park: That override is something we can test without infra changes?
[02:39] Liam O'Connor: Yes, it's a config flag in the runtime; we'll push a profile for your test rig.
[02:43] Priya Singh: About TTFT measurements — are you measuring from request arrival or after routing? We saw some network add-ons in our openwhisk front-end.
[02:50] Maya Chen: Good point. Our published TTFT is from request arrival at the Redwood edge (time we receive request) — that includes network hop to our regional edge. For Dedicated in your VPC it would be measured from your router to the instance, generally slightly lower since less network hop.
[03:04] Carlos Rivera: So dedicated could shave 20-50ms?
[03:07] Liam O'Connor: Roughly yes depending on topology. Also region proximity matters.
[03:11] Carlos Rivera: Ok. Can you walk through the latest numbers in the sheet? I see three rows for v2/v3 kernels.
[03:16] Maya Chen: Liam, do you want to summarize the sheet?
[03:18] Liam O'Connor: Sure. Quick rundown: sheet columns: kernel build, sequence mix, batch size, TTFT p50, p95, tokens/s. For your typical short-heavy mix (16-64), kernel v3 with prefix caching + streaming micro-batching yielded p50 TTFT 140ms, p95 310ms. Without streaming p50 was 180ms, p95 420ms. For the heavy 512+ mix, switching to the medium/512 kernel lowered p95 by ~90ms versus the generic kernel but reduced tokens/s by 8% on throughput runs.
[03:49] Priya Singh: The throughput drop worries our ingest pipelines. Is there a hybrid?
[03:52] Liam O'Connor: Yes, we can route by policy: latency critical routes get the streaming+512-kernel override, bulk background batches use throughput-optimized kernels or async batches. That routing can be automated by the smart router or configured by route.
[04:05] Carlos Rivera: What about quantization? We tried 4-bit earlier and saw a bit of quality drift.
[04:10] Liam O'Connor: Right, 4-bit QAT or PTQ can save latency and memory but quality varies per model. For your use-case we recommended 4-bit on non-critical models; for customer-facing flows we stuck with 8-bit quant which had negligible quality delta and still improved latency a bit. Also kernel support for 4-bit vs 8-bit differs.
[04:27] Evelyn Park: Any guidance on caching TTL for prefix keys? We worry about memory pressure on dedicated pools.
[04:33] Liam O'Connor: TTL tradeoffs: shorter TTL reduces memory but increases cold-path calls. We usually recommend LRU with a TTL tuned to your session semantics — e.g., 30-60 minutes for interactive sessions. For reserved dedicated pools we can allocate larger cache budgets.
[04:46] Carlos Rivera: Alright. Can you explain the streaming test you propose?
[04:50] Maya Chen: Liam, outline test plan.
[04:52] Liam O'Connor: We'll provision a streaming harness that mimics your front-end: same seq length mix and arrival patterns. Two runs: 1) streaming enabled with prefix caching and micro-batching, 2) baseline non-streaming with same kernel. Collect TTFT p50/p95, tokens/s, CPU/GPU utilization. We'll run both on hosted and on Dedicated replica to compare. We should get results within 48 hours.
[05:12] Priya Singh: Great. For Dedicated, do you need any network credentials?
[05:15] Maya Chen: For Dedicated we have a deployment checklist — but for the immediate streaming test we can use hosted ephemeral infra. For Dedicated PoC we'll coordinate with your infra team and use VPC peering or a private endpoint.
[05:25] Carlos Rivera: On security, we need SOC2 docs and proof of KMS integration for encryption.
[05:29] Maya Chen: We'll share the SOC2 pack and KMS integration notes after the call. Add that as an action item.
[05:33] Evelyn Park: Also SSO and RBAC for the console — can you confirm SAML 2.0?
[05:37] Maya Chen: Yes SAML 2.0 supported, plus SCIM for provisioning. We'll include those links.
[05:42] Carlos Rivera: Cool. Anything surprising in the metrics?
[05:44] Liam O'Connor: One detail: we saw a small serialization overhead when you have many small concurrent sessions due to auth/token lookup in the edge; caching tokens at the edge would shave maybe 10-15ms. Priya, is that feasible in your env?
[05:58] Priya Singh: Yes, we can add short-lived token caching; we'll coordinate.
[06:02] Carlos Rivera: So to recap, we want a streaming test with prefix caching, kernel override to favor 512 path, and a compare to baseline.
[06:09] Maya Chen: Correct. We'll run tests on hosted and a dedicated-like topology if possible.
[06:13] Priya Singh: Also we'll provide the sequence distribution file and sample traces by tomorrow.
[06:17] Liam O'Connor: Perfect. I'll also include the exact runtime flags to set: --kernel-prefer=512, --prefix-cache-ttl=3600 (we can tweak), and streaming=false/true toggles.
[06:29] Carlos Rivera: Any expected p95 after these changes?
[06:31] Liam O'Connor: Based on prior runs I'd put p50 around 120-150ms and p95 around 250-320ms for your mix on hosted with streaming and prefix caching. Dedicated likely trims another 20-40ms p95 depending on network. Not a guarantee but expectation.
[06:45] Evelyn Park: Sounds reasonable. About instrumentation, can you add trace ids to responses so we can map requests in our APM?
[06:50] Maya Chen: Yes we can add trace headers — we'll include the header spec in the notes.
[06:54] Carlos Rivera: Last question: if we enable streaming, do you support function/tool calling /structured output? We rely on JSON outputs for some flows.
[07:01] Liam O'Connor: Streaming supports structured output but we do recommend ensuring the model flushes JSON objects in chunks; sometimes streaming partial JSON can be messy but function calling mode buffers and then emits results. We can test that in the streaming harness.
[07:18] Priya Singh: Alright that's helpful.
[07:20] Maya Chen: Any blockers on the customer side for us to run the tests?
[07:23] Priya Singh: Just sharing traces and permission for the hosted run — otherwise good.
[07:27] Carlos Rivera: Ok.
[07:28] Maya Chen: Great — we'll do the runs, update the sheet, and follow up with SOC2 and SAML docs.

CLOSING / NEXT STEPS (verbal recap):
- Redwood to run streaming vs baseline tests with kernel override favoring 512 path. Expected results within 48 hours.
- HarborTrust to share trace/seq distribution by 2026-12-02.
- Redwood to share SOC2/KMS/SAML docs and updated benchmark sheet by 2026-12-02.
- Owners and deadlines captured in action items.

END OF TRANSCRIPT
